rows.Description:
The Kiowa Black Leggings Warrior Society is a 20th century revival of the Ton-Kon-Gah, one of several military societies active among the Kiowa in the 19th century. For as long as anyone can remember, warriors and veterans have held one of the most respected places in the culture of the Kiowa tribe of Oklahoma. In 1958, a group of Kiowa veterans reactivated the ancient Ton-Kon-Gah to recognize the current military service of community members. The organization has prospered over the last 50 years and has become a revered and integral part of traditional Kiowa life. 

In the series, producer Charles “Boots” Kennedye (Kiowa) interviews respected Kiowa leaders in the organization. Episode 4 includes Veteran interview with Vanessa Jennings, who dances at the ceremonial to honor her uncle, George Mopope, who at the age of 15, with the permission of his family, joined the service and fought in Korea. Jennings serves in the women’s auxiliary and takes part in the scalp dance to honor the warriors in her family and tribe.

rows.Main Title: Voyage Home: Hawai'iloa's Northwest Journey, The
rows.Description: Chronicles the historic journey of the Polynesian voyaging canoe, Hawaiʻiloa, as it sailed from Seattle, Washington to Juneau, Alaska in the summer of 1995. The voyage was a true homecoming for the Hawaiʻiloa. Its twin hulls were carved from 400-year-old spruce trees donated by the Tlingit, Haida and Tsimshian nations of Canada and Alaska and by the Sealaska Corporation. The passage of the canoe through the native villages of the Northwest Inside Passage united thousands of indigenous peoples in an unprecedented celebration of their heritage and culture.

rows.Description:
"Walela Live in Concert" is an inspirational musical journey of the spirit, recorded live in Dallas at the Kalita Humphreys Theatre, featuring the talents of Rita Coolidge, Priscilla Coolidge and Laura Satterfield singing 12 of their most memorable songs. The film gives a close-up experience of the group in a natural and inspired manner.

Walela means “hummingbird” in Cherokee. A Hummingbird is a small, but powerful symbol to many Native American tribes. The music group Walela began as a promise made by Rita and Priscilla Coolidge to their grandmother, to use their voices to honor Native Americans.

It won Best Music Video at the 2005 Native American Music Awards.

Worlds collide in the Tongass Forest, when the Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act turns tribes into corporations and sparks a lengthy logging frenzy. A story of division and redemption plays out between a Tlingit brother and sister, showing the possibility of healing both the forest and the native community.

Dr. Arne Vainio is an Ojibwe physician who works on the Fond du Lac Reservation in northern Minnesota. Frustrated by middle-aged Native men not coming in for health screenings, he came to the realization that he was also avoiding the necessary screenings. The program is based on Dr. Vainio’s 49th and 50th years of life, a critical turning point in the lives of many American Indian males when it is important to become earnestly involved in finding out more about the ways in which their health and well-being are at risk and developing ways to practice healthier choices.

rows.Description:
In the 1970s, with the swagger of unapologetic Indianness, organizers of the American Indian Movement (AIM) fought for Native liberation and survival as a community of extended families. 

Warrior Women is the story of Madonna Thunder Hawk, one such AIM leader who shaped a kindred group of activists' children - including her daughter Marcy - into the "We Will Remember" Survival School as a Native alternative to government-run education. Together, Madonna and Marcy fought for Native rights in an environment that made them more comrades than mother-daughter. Today, with Marcy now a mother herself, both are still at the forefront of Native issues, fighting against the environmental devastation of the Dakota Access Pipeline and for Indigenous cultural values. 

Through a circular Indigenous style of storytelling, this film explores what it means to navigate a movement and motherhood and how activist legacies are passed down and transformed from generation to generation in the context of colonizing government that meets Native resistance with violence.

rows.Description: The third program is a contemporary look at two communities often overlooked in the race dialogue: American Indians and Native Hawaiians. On the Pine Ridge Reservation in South Dakota, the program features the voices of three generations of Lakota families as they consider their past, their future and the process of merging multiple world views, ways of life, and ideas of America. Through the stories of these families the film considers the historical construction of Indian "otherness" and its influence on the ways a new generation of Lakota people will address issues of unemployment, alcohol, domestic abuse, and apathy ravaging their community. Meanwhile, across the Pacific Ocean, beginning in the late 1990s, lawsuit after lawsuit challenged the rights of Native Hawaiians to run schools and housing programs that provided only for their beleaguered community. Having been accused of reverse-racism, how do they see themselves in relation to the rest of the nation? And what are their connections to other Native communities?
Through untold stories of the intricate creation and often political sales of Navajo rugs, Weaving Worlds discloses the intimate portrait of economic and cultural survival through art.

rows.Main Title: Wesakechak and the First Indian People (Program 10)
rows.Description: Wesakechak asked the Creator to give him and the other animals new names. The Creator agreed to have a naming ceremony the following day, and Wesakechak's troubles began.

Wesakechak discovers why chickadees have some medicine berries and he tricks the birds into giving him some. Although he is given careful instructions, Wesakechak abuses the power of the medicine berries and gets himself into trouble.

Long ago Whiskey Jack(Kweekweeseu) thought he was very ugly, so he hid in the forest and grew very lonely. One day he asked Wesakechak for help. Unfortunately things did not work out for Kweekweeweseu the way he had hoped.

An Eastern Shoshone Elder and two Northern Arapaho youth living on the Wind River Indian Reservation attempt to learn why thousands of ancestral artifacts are in the darkness of underground archives of museums and churches, boxed away and forgotten. Like millions of indigenous people in many parts of the world, they do not control their own material culture. It is being preserved, locked away, by ‘outsiders’ who themselves do not know what they have.

rows.Description: In the heart of what was once Pawnee Indian Country - Genoa, Nebraska - was built the U.S Indian School, a government supported military style school for Indian Children from more than 20 tribes.

This documentary, narrated by Academy Award winner Linda Hunt and directed by Jed Riffe, tells the story of how the discovery of a 9,000-year-old skeleton on the banks of the Columbia River near Kennewick, Washington, reignited the conflict between anthropologists and Native peoples over the control of human remains found on ancestral Indigenous lands.

Who She Is tells the story of four individual women caught in the epidemic of Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women (MMIW). By bringing these missing women back, through animation and first-person storytelling, this film gives new life to the people buried in the statistics. Audiences will learn each woman's loves and losses and will come to know their stories. Through these women, the documentary shines a light on the wider MMIW epidemic and gendered violence in Wyoming and beyond.

rows.Description: Ed meets Kauaʻi farmer Valerie Kaneshiro, part-Japanese and Native American, who returns to the reservation to reunite with a culture she has longed for her entire life. It is a time of revitalization and reaffirmation, a celebration of indigenous food culture and a way of life. This is a story of what was nearly lost and now has been re-found.

rows.Description: A documentary marking the 10th anniversary of the founding of the FIRST Robotics Competition. FIRST (For Inspiration and Recognition of Science and Technology), a nationwide high school robotics program, was the brainchild of world-famous inventor Dean Kamen. It challenges teenagers and their adult mentors to design, prototype, and build functional robots in just six weeks, then test them against one another in regional and national competitions. Hosted by popular science and technology correspondent Dr. Michael Guillen, the program follows three teams as they deal with the complexities of building and refining 125-pound remote-controlled robots, manage the logistics of getting them and their team delivered safely to designated playing fields, and struggle with the vagaries of head-to-head competition.

rows.Description: WITHOUT A WHISPER - KANON:KWE is an untold story of how Indigenous women influenced the early suffragists in their fight for freedom and equality.  Mohawk Clan Mother Louise Herne and Professor Sally Roesch Wagner shake the foundation of the established history of the women’s rights movement in the United States. rows.Description:
In 1970, a young American Indian rock band burst upon the music scene. They carried a message of unity, hope, and truth to Indian people across America. Their lyrics brought to the surface the injustice that had been and continues to be inflicted upon Native America. They not only brought rock and roll to Indian people, they brought Indian consciousness to the world through rock and roll.

XIT Without Reservation captures their 30th-anniversary reunion concert, performed at Mystic Lake Casino in front of an appreciative audience, and featuring popular songs like "Coming of the Whiteman," "War Cry," "Nihaa Shil Hozho," and "Reservation of Education." XIT Without Reservation is perhaps the highest energy live concert special to emerge from the American Indian music scene. Thirty years after XIT signed with Motown Records and toured the U.S. and the world, founder and lead vocalist Tom Bee and band veterans Obie Sullivan (keyboards), PJ West (drums, Willie Bluehouse Johnson (lead guitar), and Louie Lomativu (bass guitar) delivered an electrifying performance with a message that still speaks to the heart of the American Indian experience to this day.
Grandfather tells the children the story of "The Corn Maidens" that evening as they sit in the tepee.

Woonspe is the Dakota word for "lesson." This program explores the problem of Native American education. It examines the historical significance and advantages and disadvantages of the four school systems available to Native Americans: BIA boarding schools, public schools, tribal contract schools, and mission schools. Produced by South Dakota ETV.

Words from a Bear examines the enigmatic life and mind of Pulitzer Prize-winning author, Navarro Scott Momaday. This profile delves into the psyche behind one of Native America’s most celebrated authors of poetry and prose. Words from a Bear visually captures the essence of Momaday’s writings, relating each written line to his unique American experience representing ancestry, place, and oral history.

rows.Main Title: Words of Life - People of Rivers (Program 9)
rows.Description: Serves as an introduction to the history of the seven tribes and a map for future growth. It offers a new perspective on Indian history, past, and future, rather than the conventional historical survey of battles and defeats.

"Words of Life - People of Rivers" serves as an introduction to the history of seven tribes and as a map for future growth. It is a good foundation for in-depth studies of each tribe, offering a new perspective on Indian history, past and future.

We Shall Remain is a provocative multi-media project that establishes Native history as an essential part of American history. The centerpiece of this initiative is a television series that tells five heartbreaking yet inspiring stories. Together, they highlight Native ingenuity and resilience over the course of 300 years. The series upends two-dimensional stereotypes of American Indians as simply ferocious warriors or peaceable lovers of the land.

Episode 5 (Wounded Knee): In 1973, members of the American Indian Movement and Oglala Lakota activists occupied the town of Wounded Knee to protest corruption, injustice, and decades of broken promises. The 71-day standoff drew national and international attention, evoking memories of the 1890 massacre at the same site. Through the lens of this dramatic confrontation, the episode traces the rise of modern Native activism and the conditions that fueled it. The occupation ultimately reaffirmed Native peoples’ enduring presence and political power in contemporary America.

rows.Description: Young Lakota  is a coming of age story following three young people as they try to forge a better future for their tribe while securing their own well being.  Sunny Clifford, her twin sister, Serena, and Brandon Ferguson are neighbors in Kyle, a small town in the heart of the Pine Ridge Reservation. Their political awakening begins when Cecelia Fire Thunder, the first female President of their tribe, defies a South Dakota law criminalizing abortion by threatening to build a women’s clinic on the sovereign territory of the reservation. In the subsequent political storm, Sunny, Serena and Brandon make choices that define who they are, and what kind of adults they will become.

rows.Description: At the confluence of the Colorado and Gila Rivers in southwestern Arizona, the rivers narrow to form a natural crossing that has been used since the first people arrived here more than 1,000 years ago. In the centuries that followed, the Yuma Crossing witnessed an extraordinary procession of peoples from diverse cultures and walks of life. The beautiful program traces the history of the Yuma Crossing from the prehistoric times to the opening of the Ocean to Ocean Highway Bridge in 1916. Produced by Yuma Crossing Foundation.
